data.q: What is the syntax for declaring a generic function in Go?
data.e: Go uses square brackets for type parameters: func MyFunc[T any](x T) T. The type parameter list appears after the function name and before the regular parameter list.

data.q: Which keyword is used to define a type constraint interface in Go generics?
data.e: In Go, constraints are defined using interfaces (often with the 'interface' keyword or by embedding existing interfaces). There is no separate 'constraint' keyword.

data.q: What does the 'any' identifier represent in a type parameter constraint?
o: A placeholder for a specific type
data.e: 'any' is a predeclared identifier that is an alias for the empty interface (interface{}). It allows any type to be used as the type argument.

data.q: How do you specify multiple type parameters in a generic function?
o: func Foo[T, U any](t T, u U)
func Foo[T any, U any](t T, u U)
func Foo[T, U](t T, u U)
func Foo[T any; U any](t T, u U)
data.e: Multiple type parameters are separated by commas within the same brackets: func Foo[T, U any](t T, u U).

data.q: Which of the following is a valid type constraint using the 'comparable' interface?
o: func Min[T comparable](a, b T) T
func Min[T == comparable](a, b T) T
func Min[T implements comparable](a, b T) T
func Min[T : comparable](a, b T) T
data.e: The 'comparable' interface is a predeclared constraint that allows types supporting == and !=. It is used directly in the type parameter list.

data.q: What is type inference in Go generics?
o: The compiler deduces type arguments from function arguments
The programmer explicitly provides type arguments
The type parameters are ignored during compilation
data.e: Go supports type inference: when calling a generic function, you can omit explicit type arguments if the compiler can infer them from the regular function arguments.

data.q: How do you instantiate a generic type with explicit type arguments?
data.e: To instantiate a generic type, provide the type argument in square brackets after the type name: MyGenericType[int]{}.

data.q: What is the purpose of a type set in a constraint interface?
o: To list all allowed concrete types for a type parameter
To define methods that the type must implement
To specify the memory layout of the type
To declare the zero value of the type
data.e: A constraint interface defines a type set — the set of types that satisfy the constraint. It can include method requirements and type terms (using the '|' union operator) to explicitly list allowed types.

data.q: Which operator is used in a constraint interface to denote a union of types?
data.e: The '|' operator in an interface used as a constraint creates a union of types (type terms). For example: interface { int | float64 }.

data.q: Can a generic type have methods with their own type parameters?
o: Yes, methods can declare additional type parameters
No, methods cannot have type parameters
Only if the receiver is a pointer
data.e: Methods on generic types can have their own type parameters, independent of the receiver's type parameters. This is sometimes called 'generic methods'.

data.q: What is the zero value of a generic type parameter T?
o: The zero value of the concrete type substituted for T
data.e: A variable of type T takes the zero value of the concrete type argument provided at instantiation. For example, if T is int, zero is 0; if T is *string, zero is nil.

data.q: Which package provides commonly used constraints like 'comparable', 'Ordered', etc.?
data.e: The package golang.org/x/exp/constraints (now also available as 'constraints' in the standard library since Go 1.21) provides predefined constraints such as Ordered, Signed, Unsigned, Integer, Float, and Complex.

data.q: What happens if you use a type argument that does not satisfy the constraint?
data.e: Go performs constraint checking at compile time. If a type argument does not satisfy the constraint, the code will not compile.

data.q: Can you use a generic type as a receiver in a method declaration?
o: Yes, e.g., func (s Stack[T]) Push(v T)
No, receivers must be concrete types
Only if the type is an interface
data.e: Generic types can be used as receivers. The method can also have additional type parameters.

data.q: What is the difference between 'any' and 'comparable' constraints?
o: 'any' allows any type; 'comparable' allows only types supporting == and !=.
'any' requires types to have methods; 'comparable' does not
data.e: 'any' (alias for interface{}) accepts all types. 'comparable' only accepts types that are comparable with == and != (e.g., not slices, maps, functions).

data.q: In Go 1.18+, which of the following is a valid generic type definition?
o: type Pair[T, U any] struct { First T; Second U }
type Pair[T, U] struct { First T; Second U }
type Pair[T any, U any] struct { First T; Second U }
type Pair<T, U> struct { First T; Second U }
data.e: Generic type definitions use square brackets with type parameters and optional constraints: type Pair[T, U any] struct { ... }.
